en.title: Hausa: the whole course
en.short: What Hausa studies covers, how Hausa degrees are organised, the main areas and how to study them.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text:
Hausa is a Chadic language of the Afroasiatic family and one of the largest languages of West Africa. It is spoken mainly in northern Nigeria and southern Niger, and also in communities in Chad, Cameroon, Benin, Ghana and Sudan. It has long been written in Boko, a Latin-based script, and Ajami, an Arabic-based script, and it is a major language of trade, religion, media and education.

Hausa studies is the degree in the language, its linguistics, literature and culture. You study how the language sounds and is written, how words and sentences are built, how people use it in society, and the oral and written literature speakers have produced. The notes are in English, with Hausa examples. Give a Hausa word only when you are sure of its spelling and tone marks; otherwise explain in English.

sections.heading: How a degree is organised
sections.text:
In Nigeria, a BA Hausa is commonly a four-year programme. Many universities offer it as a single honours degree, and some offer combined honours with another subject, such as English or education. Colleges of education offer the NCE (Nigeria Certificate in Education) for teaching Hausa. Postgraduate awards include MA, MPhil and PhD. Titles and entry requirements vary.

In Niger, Hausa is studied within arts and human sciences programmes, and award titles differ. Elsewhere, including Ghana and Cameroon, it is taught in some universities within African languages, linguistics or area studies. Do not assume one country’s structure fits another.

Lengths and course lists change. Check your departmental handbook and your national regulator or awarding body. In Nigeria the National Universities Commission guides university programmes, but your own handbook lists what to register for.

sections.heading: Main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Most programmes begin with introduction to Hausa studies. You then learn the sound system, orthography in Boko and Ajami, morphology and basic syntax, alongside oral literature, culture and society, reading and composition, and a first course in general linguistics.

The core years deepen the language: tone and morphophonology, the verb system and aspect, complex sentences, semantics and pragmatics, dialectology, historical and comparative linguistics, lexicography, translation and interpreting, sociolinguistics, and language planning and Hausa in education. Literature and culture run alongside: prose fiction, poetry oral and written, drama and performance, literary criticism and theory, media and popular culture, and Islamic scholarship and Hausa literature. Research methods usually come before the final project.

At master’s level the work is more research-led: advanced phonology and morphosyntax, advanced literary theory and comparative poetics, language contact and change, and research methods and dissertation design.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Start with sound and tone. Hausa uses tone and vowel length to distinguish words, so learn them from the first week. Listen to recordings by first-language speakers, repeat aloud, and write tone marks and vowel length in your vocabulary book. Do not rely on English spelling.

Read Hausa of several kinds: news, stories, poems and plays. Keep a notebook of new words with a sentence for each. For literature, learn the title, the author, the form and one or two main themes, and read at least one work in Hausa rather than only in translation.

For linguistics, practise with data. Take a short set of Hausa words or sentences and work out the pattern yourself before reading the answer. Rules and policies on language in education differ by country and change, so check the current official source.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Many students ignore tone and vowel length, then wonder why words look the same. Others copy Hausa spellings from English sources without checking the standard orthography.

In linguistics, a common fault is describing English grammar and calling it Hausa grammar. Another is treating one dialect as the whole language. Hausa has real regional variation, and standard written Hausa is a convention, not the only form.

In literature, students often summarise a plot and call it criticism, or quote a translated text as if it were the original. In research, the usual faults are a topic too broad to finish, sources that are never cited, and conclusions that go beyond the evidence collected.

keyPoints: Hausa studies covers the Hausa language, its linguistics, literature and culture.
Hausa is written in both Boko and Ajami, and both are part of the course.
Degree length and award titles differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook.
Tone and vowel length change meaning in Hausa, so learn them from the first week.
Read real Hausa texts, not only English translations or descriptions.
Name the country whenever you state a rule, policy or curriculum about language in education.

en.title: Introduction to Hausa Studies
en.short: What the Hausa degree covers, its main branches, study skills, sources and citation.

sections.heading: The field
sections.text:
Hausa Studies is the academic study of the Hausa language, its literature and its culture. Hausa is a Chadic language in the Afroasiatic family, spoken mainly in northern Nigeria and southern Niger and widely used as a second language in West Africa. The degree brings together three broad branches: linguistics, literary study and cultural history. Linguistics is the systematic study of language; literary study examines creative texts and their forms; cultural history studies shared practices, beliefs and institutions.

They overlap, but ask different questions.

sections.heading: Branches and terms
sections.text:
Within linguistics, students meet phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics and sociolinguistics. Within literature, they study oral and written forms, genres and criticism. Cultural history draws on history, anthropology, religion and media studies.

A key term is register, the variety of language used in a particular situation, such as formal writing. Another is genre, a recognised type of text or performance. Students also learn to distinguish descriptive study from language learning. Descriptive study analyses how Hausa works; language learning trains you to use it. The degree includes both, but they differ.

sections.heading: Study skills and sources
sections.text:
Read primary texts in Hausa where you can, and keep a vocabulary notebook with full spellings. Use grammars, dictionaries and scholarly books and articles. For oral material, record the narrator, place, date and permission. Cite every source.

Follow your department’s required style, such as author-date or footnotes, and give page numbers for quotations. A small case: if you collect a proverb, note who said it, where and when, then compare it with a published collection.

sections.heading: How the parts fit
sections.text:
Linguistics explains the language of a text; literary study explains its form and effect; cultural history explains its setting and audience.

A praise poem, for example, can be analysed for its sounds and grammar, its imagery, and its place in a court or community. Keep description separate from evaluation: first say what the text or speech does, then judge it. This habit protects accuracy and makes your writing easier to defend.

keyPoints: Hausa Studies covers the Hausa language, its literature and its culture.
Hausa is a Chadic language of the Afroasiatic family, spoken mainly in northern Nigeria and southern Niger.
Linguistics, literary study and cultural history are distinct but overlapping branches.
Descriptive study analyses how Hausa works; language learning trains you to use it.
Use scholarly sources, record oral sources fully, and cite every source in your department’s style.
Keep description separate from evaluation when analysing texts or speech.

en.title: The Hausa Sound System: Phonetics and Phonology
en.short: Hausa consonants, vowels and vowel length, tone, syllables, and telling sounds from letters.

sections.heading: Sounds and letters
sections.text:
Phonetics studies the physical sounds of speech; phonology studies how a language organises them into units that carry meaning. A phoneme is a sound that can change meaning in a language. Hausa is a Chadic language in the Afroasiatic family, spoken mainly in northern Nigeria and in neighbouring Niger.

Writing is not the same as sound. In standard Boko, the Latin-based Hausa writing system, two letters can write one sound: sh, ts and 'y are each single sounds. Tone is usually not written in ordinary text, so a reader must know the word already.

sections.heading: Consonants
sections.text:
Hausa has a large consonant inventory. Four consonants are glottalised, made with a constriction or closure in the throat: ɓ, ɗ, ts and ƙ. There is also a palatalised glottal stop, written 'y. These contrast with plain b, d, t, k and y, so the wrong one gives a different word or no word at all.

Other consonants include c, pronounced like ch in church, j as in judge, and sh. Hausa also has labialised and palatalised consonants such as kw and ky.

sections.heading: Vowels and length
sections.text:
Hausa has five vowel qualities, a, e, i, o and u, and each can be short or long. Long vowels are written double in Boko, as in aa; linguistic transcription may use a macron.

Length changes meaning. A commonly cited pair is gari, town, and gaari, flour. Say each vowel at its true length; shortening a long vowel, or lengthening a short one, can turn one word into another.

sections.heading: Tone and syllables
sections.text:
Hausa is a tone language. It has High and Low level tones, and a falling tone on long vowels. Tone is marked with an acute accent for High, as in á, and a grave accent for Low, as in à. Tone can be grammatical: the pronoun nàa with Low tone marks continuing action, while náa with High tone marks completed action.

A syllable is usually consonant plus vowel, consonant plus long vowel, or consonant-vowel-consonant at the end of a word. Consonant clusters do not begin a syllable. In transcription, write one symbol for each sound: sh is [ʃ], c is [tʃ].

keyPoints: Phonetics studies speech sounds; phonology studies how a language organises them.
A phoneme is a sound whose substitution changes meaning.
Hausa has glottalised ɓ, ɗ, ts, ƙ and 'y, which contrast with plain b, d, t, k and y.
Every Hausa vowel is short or long, and length can change meaning, as in gari and gaari.
Hausa has High and Low tones, marked á and à, and tone can be grammatical.
Hausa syllables are CV, CVV or word-final CVC; clusters do not begin a syllable.

en.title: Hausa Orthography and Writing Systems: Boko and Ajami
en.short: Boko and Ajami scripts, Hausa spelling, special letters, vowel and tone marking, and their uses.

sections.heading: Two scripts
sections.text: Boko is the Latin-based alphabet used for standard Hausa. Ajami is the tradition of writing Hausa in Arabic script. Boko is the main script for schools, newspapers and official publishing in Nigeria and Niger, though policy differs by country. Ajami is older in the region and grew with Islamic literacy. It is still used in Quranic schools, religious texts, personal letters and local records. Each script has its own spelling habits.

sections.heading: Boko spelling
sections.text: The standard Boko alphabet uses ordinary Latin letters plus hooked letters ɓ, ɗ, ƙ and ƴ, with ƴ often typed as 'y. Digraphs sh and ts each stand for one consonant. Long vowels are usually written double: aa, ee, ii, oo, uu. Short vowels are single. Vowel length can change meaning: wa means to or for, while waa means who. Learn hooked letters as separate letters, not decorated k, d or b: for example, ƙasaa, meaning land, begins with hooked ƙ, a different consonant from k.

sections.heading: Tone and reading
sections.text: Tone is part of Hausa pronunciation, but everyday Boko often leaves it unmarked. Dictionaries and teaching texts may mark high tone with an acute accent (á) and low tone with a grave accent (à). Falling tone can be shown by a circumflex (â) in some works. Read the dictionary’s key before copying accents, because conventions vary. In examinations, follow your department’s style. Do not add tone marks at random: a wrong mark can mislead a reader.

sections.heading: History and uses
sections.text: Ajami uses Arabic letters, with added dots or combinations for Hausa sounds absent from Arabic. Vowel signs may be written, but tone is not marked consistently, and spelling varies between schools and regions. Ajami is common in Islamic education, poetry, charms, medical notes and family archives. Boko became dominant in colonial and post-colonial schooling and print. In Nigeria, standard Hausa in education and the media is normally Boko; Ajami remains important in religious and traditional life. In Niger, both scripts have public uses. Check the current official orthography for the country concerned.

keyPoints: Boko is the Latin-based standard Hausa script; Ajami is the Arabic-based tradition.
Standard Boko uses hooked letters ɓ, ɗ, ƙ and ƴ, plus digraphs sh and ts.
Long vowels are usually written double in Boko, and vowel length can change meaning.
Tone is often unmarked in everyday Boko but may be shown with accents in dictionaries and teaching texts.
Ajami adapts Arabic letters for Hausa sounds and is used mainly in Islamic and traditional settings.
Boko dominates formal education and media in Nigeria, but official policy and practice differ by country.

en.title: Hausa Morphology: Word Structure and Word Formation
en.short: Roots, affixes, reduplication, inflection, derivation, noun plurals, gender and word classes in Hausa.

sections.heading: Roots and affixes
sections.text:
Morphology studies how words are built. The root is the core part that carries the main meaning. An affix is a bound form added to a root or stem: a prefix before it, a suffix after it. Hausa uses prefixes, suffixes and reduplication, which repeats all or part of a word. Reduplication can mark plurality, intensity or repetition.

To segment a word, compare related forms and separate the constant part from the changing part.

sections.heading: Inflection and derivation
sections.text:
Inflection makes grammatical forms of the same word without changing its basic meaning or word class. In Hausa, noun plurals and verb forms for aspect are inflectional. Derivation makes a new word, often different class, by adding an affix or changing the pattern. An agent noun may come from a verb; an abstract noun from an adjective.

The test is meaning and class: a new name is derivation, a grammatical fit is inflection. Morphology ends at the word; syntax begins when words combine.

sections.heading: Nouns: plurals and gender
sections.text:
Hausa nouns have grammatical gender: masculine or feminine. Gender is a property of the noun that controls agreement on pronouns, adjectives and demonstratives. It is not the same as natural sex, and a noun’s ending does not always show it. Plurals are complex. Hausa has many plural patterns, using different suffixes, vowel changes and irregular forms. There is no single plural rule like English -s, so learn each noun with its plural.

For example, the Hausa word for 'book' changes its vowels in the plural; the word for 'house' takes a suffix.

sections.heading: Word classes and segmentation
sections.text:
The main word classes are nouns, verbs, adjectives, pronouns, adverbs, prepositions, conjunctions, particles and ideophones (vivid descriptive words). Identify a class by behaviour: what it can follow, what inflection it takes, and its phrase work. Do not decide from meaning alone.

When you segment, write the word, mark the root, and label each affix. Keep morphology separate from syntax: a plural suffix is morphology; a plural pronoun agreeing with a noun is syntax.

keyPoints: Morphology studies word structure; syntax studies how words combine.
A root carries the core meaning; affixes and reduplication build new forms.
Inflection makes grammatical forms of one word; derivation makes a new word.
Hausa nouns have masculine or feminine gender, shown mainly by agreement.
Hausa plural patterns are many and must be learned with each noun.
Segment a word by comparing related forms and separating root from affixes.

en.title: Basic Hausa Syntax: Simple Clauses
en.short: Hausa word order, noun phrases, verbal and non-verbal clauses, questions and negation.

sections.heading: Word order
sections.text:
Basic Hausa declarative clauses are Subject–Verb–Object (SVO), as in English: subject first, then the verb, then the object. Hausa also marks the subject inside the verb complex with an agreement word, so the subject noun phrase can be left out when it is clear. 'Yara sun ci abinci' means the children ate food; 'sun ci abinci' means they ate food.

Tone marks are omitted in these examples; check a dictionary for them.

sections.heading: Noun phrases
sections.text:
A noun phrase is built around a head noun. The head usually comes first: adjectives follow it and agree with it in gender and number, while possessive suffixes follow it and agree with the possessor. Hausa nouns are masculine or feminine, singular or plural. Demonstratives come before or after the noun: 'wannan' (this) precedes it, while 'nan' (this) follows it, as in 'littafin nan' (this book).

A noun phrase can act as subject, object or predicate. To parse a clause, name the head of each phrase and its job.

sections.heading: Verbal and non-verbal clauses
sections.text:
A verbal clause has a verb as its predicate. A non-verbal or nominal clause has no verb: its predicate is a noun, adjective or prepositional phrase. Present-time identification uses the copula particles 'ne' (masculine) and 'ce' (feminine) after the predicate: 'shi malami ne' he is a teacher; 'ita malama ce' she is a teacher.

'Akwai' states existence (there is); 'babu' denies it (there is not).

sections.heading: Questions and negation
sections.text:
Yes/no questions are marked mainly by rising intonation, sometimes with 'ko'. Content questions begin with a question word: 'wa' (who), 'me' (what), 'ina' (where), 'yaushe' (when), 'don me' (why).

Verbal negation is discontinuous: a negative auxiliary form comes before the verb and 'ba' closes the clause, as in 'ban ci abinci ba' (I did not eat food). 'Ba ... da' negates possession: 'ba ni da kudi' (I have no money).

keyPoints: Basic Hausa declarative order is Subject–Verb–Object.
The verb complex carries an agreement word for the subject, so the subject noun phrase can be dropped.
In a noun phrase the head noun comes first; adjectives follow it and agree with it in gender and number.
Non-verbal clauses have no verb; 'ne' and 'ce' link a predicate to its subject.
Yes/no questions use intonation; content questions start with a question word.
Verbal negation is discontinuous: the auxiliary takes a negative form before the verb, and 'ba' closes the clause.

en.title: Introduction to Hausa Oral Literature
en.short: Genres, performance, transmission, and how oral texts are collected, transcribed and analysed.

sections.heading: What oral literature is
sections.text: Oral literature is spoken or sung art that lives in performance. It includes stories, sayings, riddles and songs passed on by memory and by example. It is not simply written literature read aloud. A written text is usually fixed by an author and read privately. An oral text changes with each telling, and the audience helps shape it through replies, laughter or correction. The performer may also adapt length and detail to the occasion.

sections.heading: Main genres
sections.text: Folktales are fictional stories, often with animal tricksters, told for entertainment and teaching. Proverbs are short, fixed sayings that carry accepted wisdom and are used to argue, advise or soften a point. Riddles are questions or statements with hidden answers, used to test wit and teach vocabulary. Praise songs honour people, families or occupations. Work songs set rhythm for shared labour and reduce fatigue. Genres overlap: a tale may contain proverbs and songs.

sections.heading: Performance and transmission
sections.text: Performance means the whole event: the teller, audience, place, time, voice, gesture and music. Transmission happens through families, age groups, ceremonies and professional performers. Memory is helped by formulas, repeated phrases, rhythm and call-and-response. The audience is not passive. It may answer a call, clap, laugh or ask for more. A concrete case: suppose a student records a folktale at a ceremony in Kano. The recording shows the teller pausing while listeners answer. The transcription must mark those pauses and replies, not only the teller’s words.

sections.heading: Collecting and analysis
sections.text: Collection begins with permission and respect for the performer. Record the event, note date, place, performers and audience, and keep the original file. Transcription writes down the words, including tone marks where the transcription system requires them, plus pauses, gestures and audience responses. Translation should be separate from transcription. Analysis then asks about structure, language, occasion and meaning. Fieldworkers must credit performers and follow consent rules. Oral and written literature differ in authorship, fixity and reception, but they influence each other.

keyPoints: Oral literature is performed art that changes with each telling and depends on audience response.
The main genres include folktales, proverbs, riddles, praise songs and work songs.
Performance covers the teller, audience, occasion, voice, gesture and music, not only the words.
Transmission relies on memory, example, formulas, rhythm and audience participation.
Collection requires permission, recording, metadata, transcription, separate translation and ethical credit.
Oral texts differ from written literature in authorship, fixity and reception, but the two influence each other.

en.title: Hausa Culture and Society: An Introduction
en.short: Household, marriage, religion, festivals, crafts, food, music and dress in Hausa communities.

sections.heading: Household and marriage
sections.text: Hausa society is organised around households, extended families and wider kin networks. Most households trace inheritance through the father’s line, but residence, authority and support vary between rural and urban settings and across Nigeria, Niger and the diaspora. Marriage is usually a contract under Islamic law where the parties are Muslim, combined with local custom. Bridewealth, wedding costs and the age of marriage differ by family, income and place. A custom in one town is not a rule for all Hausa people.

sections.heading: Religion and festivals
sections.text: Most Hausa people are Muslim, but not all; Hausa Christian communities exist, and some older practices survive in particular places. Islam shapes daily prayer, fasting, almsgiving, dress and the festival calendar. The two Eid festivals are widely observed, while celebrations of the Prophet’s birthday and other occasions vary by community and school of thought. Some places hold older festivals or possession ceremonies, but these are local and not universal. Religious authority differs between city and countryside.

sections.heading: Work, food and dress
sections.text: Farming, trade, crafts and wage work shape daily life. Crafts include leatherwork, weaving, embroidery, pottery and metalwork, with regional specialities. Staple foods come from millet, sorghum, maize or rice, served with soups or sauces; recipes and festive dishes vary. Dress often includes embroidered robes, wrappers and head coverings, and it changes with gender, age, occasion and Islamic norms. A market town and a rural village may differ in wedding dress, food and craft production.

sections.heading: Music, variation and language
sections.text: Music ranges from praise singing and drumming to popular styles, and its use depends on setting and religious opinion. Hausa communities were shaped by precolonial states, the Sokoto Caliphate, colonial borders and migration, so customs vary across Nigeria, Niger and the diaspora. Culture also shapes language use: greetings, address terms, proverbs and polite forms mark age, status, gender and setting. For example, invented families in Kano city and rural Maradi may both be Hausa and Muslim yet arrange weddings differently, so one local custom is not universal.

keyPoints: Hausa culture varies by place, period and community, so no single local custom represents all Hausa people.
Households and extended kin are central, but residence, inheritance and marriage arrangements vary.
Most Hausa people are Muslim, and Islam shapes festivals and dress, but not all Hausa people are Muslim.
Crafts, food, music and dress differ by region, income, occasion and religious opinion.
Precolonial states, the Sokoto Caliphate, colonial borders and migration shaped modern Hausa communities.
Language use reflects culture through greetings, address forms and polite forms that mark status and setting.

en.title: Reading and Composition in Hausa
en.short: Reading comprehension, summary, planning, letters, reports, essays and written style in Hausa.

sections.heading: Reading and summary
sections.text:
Reading comprehension means getting the main idea, supporting details and the writer’s purpose. Read a Hausa passage twice: first for the general sense, then for difficult words. Use the sentence around an unknown word to guess its meaning, then check a dictionary.

A summary restates the main points in your own words and in fewer words. Keep the order of ideas, leave out examples and repetition, and do not copy whole sentences.

sections.heading: Planning and paragraphs
sections.text:
Controlled composition is writing with a clear guide: a model text, a list of points or questions. Before writing, make an outline. Decide the purpose, the reader and the main point. A short essay needs an introduction, body paragraphs and a conclusion.

A paragraph carries one main idea. Start with a topic sentence, add details, then link to the next. Example: Amina reports a cancelled lecture to a student association. She lists the date, reason, who was told and action taken, then gives each step a short paragraph.

sections.heading: Letters and reports
sections.text:
A formal letter has the sender’s address, the receiver’s address, the date, a salutation, a clear subject, the body and a closing. An informal letter to a friend can be shorter and warmer. In both, state your purpose early and keep one main topic per paragraph.

A report presents facts for a reader who was not there. Use a clear title, say what happened, give details in logical order, and end with a short conclusion or recommendation.

sections.heading: Spelling, tone and style
sections.text:
Standard Hausa writing uses accepted Boko spelling (the Latin-based script), including hooked letters and tone marks. These marks can change meaning, so check them in a dictionary or a reliable model text. Read your draft aloud, then proofread for spelling, agreement and punctuation.

Spoken Hausa relies on gesture, repetition and shared setting. Written Hausa must be more explicit because the reader is absent. Use complete sentences, clear links and a polite, neutral tone.

keyPoints: Reading comprehension asks for the main idea, supporting details and the writer’s purpose.
A summary restates the main points in fewer words and in your own words.
Plan before writing: decide purpose, reader and outline, then draft introduction, body and conclusion.
A paragraph carries one main idea, opened by a topic sentence.
Formal letters include sender’s and receiver’s addresses, date, salutation, subject, body and closing; reports present facts in logical order.
Standard Hausa spelling and tone marks must be checked because they can change meaning, and written Hausa is more explicit than spoken Hausa.

en.title: Introduction to Linguistics for Hausa Students
en.short: This summary covers core linguistic concepts, description versus prescription, and methods for analysing Hausa.

sections.heading: What linguistics studies
sections.text: Linguistics is the systematic study of language, not a set of rules for correct speech. It asks how sounds, words and sentences are organised, how meaning is made, and how people use language in society. A first-year course introduces the main branches and the habit of basing claims on evidence. The aim is to describe Hausa as a language with its own system, not only to speak it fluently.

sections.heading: Levels of language
sections.text: Phonetics studies speech sounds as physical events: how they are produced, transmitted and heard. Phonology studies how a language organises those sounds into contrastive units and patterns. Morphology studies word structure and word formation. Syntax studies how words combine into phrases and clauses. Semantics studies meaning in language, while sociolinguistics studies variation by region, class, age, gender and situation. Historical linguistics studies change over time and relationships between languages.

sections.heading: Description and method
sections.text: A descriptive approach records how people actually speak, including variation. A prescriptive approach states how people ought to speak, often based on a standard. Linguists may study standards, but they do not confuse a standard with the whole language. Good description needs data: recorded speech, written texts or elicited examples. Transcription writes speech in a consistent symbol system, usually the International Phonetic Alphabet. For Hausa, a careful transcription marks tone and vowel length, because these can distinguish words; the full sound system has its own topic.

sections.heading: From speaking to analysis
sections.text: Analysis is an argument. The linguist states a claim, gives examples, and shows that the claim explains the data better than a rival claim. Case: Amina says a Hausa form is wrong; Musa uses it. A descriptive student asks who uses it, where, with whom, and whether it contrasts with another form. The student records examples, transcribes them, and tests a hypothesis. The conclusion may be that the form is dialectal or informal, not simply wrong.

keyPoints: Linguistics describes language systematically and bases claims on evidence.
Phonetics, phonology, morphology, syntax and semantics study different levels of language.
Sociolinguistics studies variation and use in society; historical linguistics studies change over time.
Descriptive linguistics records actual usage; prescriptive linguistics states preferred usage.
Transcription is a consistent written record of speech, and for Hausa it must mark tone and vowel length.
Linguistic analysis is an argument that compares competing explanations of the same data.

en.title: Hausa Tone and Morphophonology
en.short: Lexical and grammatical tone, noun and verb patterns, phrase tone, and boundary sound changes in Hausa.

sections.heading: Tone and contrast
sections.text:
Hausa is tonal: pitch distinguishes words. Descriptions usually recognise two level tones, High and Low, written H and L. Falling and rising contours are often analysed as sequences of level tones on one tone-bearing unit, usually a vowel.

Tone is lexical when it belongs to a word’s dictionary entry, as in a minimal pair. It is grammatical when it marks a construction such as tense, aspect, person or possession. Ordinary Boko spelling does not mark tone, and vowel length is marked inconsistently in practice, so examples need a consistent transcription.

sections.heading: Noun and verb tone
sections.text:
Nouns carry tone patterns, and the pattern is part of the lexical entry. Singular, plural and definite forms may differ in tone as well as affixes, so a plural is not just a suffix.

Verb stems also belong to tone classes. In the verb phrase, tone on subject pronouns and on the verb helps mark aspect, tense and person, alongside segmental material. The analyst separates the underlying melody from surface pitch and asks which morpheme supplies each tone.

sections.heading: Boundaries and phrases
sections.text:
At morpheme boundaries, sounds change to ease pronunciation. Vowels may assimilate in height or backness, shorten, delete, or be separated by an inserted glide. Consonants may assimilate in place or voice. Tone may spread, shift, or remain floating: a tone not pronounced on its own segment but affecting neighbouring pitch. A floating tone can explain why a suffix seems toneless in one form but changes pitch in another.

In phrases and sentences, transcribe pitch, mark H and L, and compare underlying and surface forms. Focus, negation and question marking can change a phrase’s tonal shape. A small case: take a two-syllable noun with High-Low. If a possessive gives High-High, do not assume the suffix is toneless. Posit a Low tone and test whether it appears elsewhere, or whether High has spread. Choose the simplest rule that accounts for all forms.

keyPoints: Hausa has two level tones, High and Low; contour tones are usually analysed as sequences.
Lexical tone distinguishes dictionary words, while grammatical tone marks constructions such as tense, aspect, person and possession.
Noun tone patterns and verb tone classes are part of lexical entries and interact with affixes and aspect marking.
At morpheme boundaries, vowels and consonants may assimilate, delete or take a glide, and tone may spread, shift or float.
A floating tone is not pronounced on its own segment but can affect neighbouring pitch.
Analyse phrase tone by comparing underlying melodies with surface H and L patterns across constructions.

en.title: The Hausa Verb System and Aspect
en.short: Hausa verb forms, aspect and time, person marking, particles, verb classes and connected speech.

sections.heading: Aspect not tense
sections.text: Hausa verbs mark aspect more than tense. Aspect is the speaker’s view of an event: perfective presents it as a single whole, often completed; imperfective presents it as ongoing, repeated or habitual. Time is inferred from context and adverbs. For example, Amina may use a perfective to report that she cooked once, an imperfective to say she cooks every day, and a future construction for tomorrow. A future particle adds future reference. Grammars therefore describe aspect and mood rather than a simple past-present-future system.

sections.heading: Person and particles
sections.text: Person, number and gender are usually shown by subject markers that sit before the verb. These markers often combine with aspect or mood, so one short form can signal both she and perfective. Preverbal particles mark future, habitual and negative meanings, while the subjunctive is shown by special subject pronoun forms. Auxiliaries and light verbs add grammatical meaning while the main verb carries the lexical meaning. In connected speech these markers may fuse, shorten or change tone, so the written form and the spoken form can differ.

sections.heading: Verb classes
sections.text: Hausa verbs are commonly grouped by transitivity, by tone class and by morphological grade. Grade refers to a pattern of tone and suffix that changes the meaning, for example by adding a sense of completeness. A verb may belong to more than one useful class. Learners should check a good grammar or dictionary for the grade and tone pattern of each verb, because the same consonants with different grades can carry different meanings.

sections.heading: Connected speech
sections.text: In connected speech, verb forms are affected by elision, assimilation and tone. A subject marker may lose a vowel before another vowel, and a particle may merge with the following verb. Relative and focus constructions use special relative forms of the perfective and imperfective. The same event can therefore appear in a different shape when it is placed in a relative clause or under focus. Listen for the whole phrase, not just the dictionary form of the verb.

keyPoints: Hausa marks aspect and mood more than tense; perfective views an event as a whole and imperfective as ongoing or habitual.
Time reference comes from context, adverbs and particles, not from a single past tense.
Subject markers before the verb mark person, number and gender and often fuse with aspect or mood.
Preverbal particles mark future, habitual and negative meanings; the subjunctive uses its own subject pronoun forms.
Hausa verbs are classified by transitivity, tone class and morphological grade.
In connected speech, markers may elide, assimilate or change tone, and relative forms differ from citation forms.

en.title: Complex Sentences in Hausa
en.short: Relative, complement and adverbial clauses, focus, topicalisation, coordination and subordination in Hausa.

sections.heading: Building complex sentences
sections.text:
A complex sentence has one main clause and at least one dependent clause. The dependent clause cannot stand alone; it fills a role inside the main clause or modifies it. Coordination joins clauses of equal status, usually with conjunctions meaning 'and', 'or' and 'but'. Subordination makes one clause depend on another. Hausa combines both, and clauses can be nested, so a sentence may contain several layers.

The basic clause order is subject, verb, object, but information structure can change it. The same proposition can be presented as neutral, focused or topicalised.

sections.heading: Relative and complement clauses
sections.text: Relative clauses modify a noun. In Hausa they normally follow the noun and contain a relative marker; where the modified noun is not the subject, a pronoun may refer back to it. Complement clauses fill an argument slot, especially the object of verbs of saying, thinking or knowing. They are often introduced by a complementiser meaning 'that'. Both types are subordinate: they cannot stand alone and they allow one sentence to contain another.

sections.heading: Adverbial clauses
sections.text: Adverbial clauses express time, reason, condition, purpose or concession. Hausa uses conjunctions for these meanings, and the dependent clause may come before or after the main clause. Placing it first often sets a background or frame; placing it last often adds afterthought or emphasis. The conjunction and its context decide the meaning, not the position of the clause, so learners should check each conjunction in a dictionary and in real texts.

sections.heading: Focus and order
sections.text: Focus highlights new or contrastive information. Hausa has focus markers and focus positions; a focused phrase often moves forward, and the rest of the sentence adjusts. Topicalisation sets a topic, often at the left edge, and a pronoun may resume it later. Focus answers a question such as 'who did it?'; topicalisation says what the sentence is about. Neither changes the basic truth of the proposition, but both change emphasis and word order.

keyPoints: A complex sentence contains a main clause and at least one dependent clause.
Coordination joins clauses of equal status; subordination makes one clause depend on another.
Relative clauses modify nouns and in Hausa normally follow the noun with a relative marker.
Complement clauses fill an argument slot and are often introduced by a complementiser meaning 'that'.
Adverbial clauses express time, reason, condition, purpose or concession and can move for emphasis.
Focus highlights new or contrastive information, while topicalisation sets the topic and can change word order.

en.title: Hausa Semantics and Pragmatics: Meaning in Context
en.short: Meaning relations, metaphor, idiom, politeness, speech acts, address terms and implicature in Hausa.

sections.heading: Semantics and relations
sections.text: Semantics studies literal meaning; pragmatics studies meaning in use. Meaning relations include synonymy (near-same meaning), antonymy (opposites), hyponymy (a specific term under a general one), polysemy (related senses) and homonymy (unrelated senses that share the same form, in sound or spelling). In Hausa, exact synonymy is rare: dialect, register and borrowing from Arabic and English create near-synonyms. Test relations in sentences, not from dictionary glosses alone.

sections.heading: Metaphor and idiom
sections.text: Metaphor treats one domain in terms of another; a conceptual metaphor is a pattern of thought, not only a poetic line. Many Hausa metaphors and idioms draw on farming, travel, the body, family life and Islamic learning, but they vary by region, generation and setting. An idiom is a fixed expression whose meaning is not the sum of its parts. Do not translate idioms literally. Check meaning with several speakers and note the situation of use.

sections.heading: Politeness and speech acts
sections.text: Speech act theory separates locution (what is said), illocution (the act performed, such as requesting) and perlocution (the effect). A request may be direct or indirect. Politeness concerns face, a person’s public self-image. Positive politeness shows approval; negative politeness avoids imposing. In many Hausa settings, greeting, indirectness, titles and respect terms matter across age and status. Address terms include kinship words, titles and terms of respect; choice depends on gender, age, religion, occupation and setting. Do not assume one rule for all speakers.

sections.heading: Implicature and method
sections.text: Conversational implicature is meaning suggested but not stated. Grice’s cooperative principle (the assumption that speakers aim to make their contributions helpful) and maxims of quantity, quality, relation and manner explain how hearers infer it; flouting a maxim produces an implicature. Example, in English gloss: Amina asks Musa, 'Is the tea ready?' Musa replies, 'The water is boiling.' He does not say no, but the reply implicates that the tea is not ready yet. The inference depends on shared knowledge of tea-making. To analyse Hausa data, record natural talk with context, note speaker, setting and relationship, check interpretations with native speakers, and compare variants. Avoid overgeneralising from one example or one region.

keyPoints: Semantics studies literal meaning; pragmatics studies meaning in use.
Meaning relations include synonymy, antonymy, hyponymy, polysemy and homonymy; exact synonymy is rare in Hausa.
Metaphors are patterns of thought; idioms are fixed expressions and should not be translated literally.
Speech act theory separates locution, illocution and perlocution; politeness and address terms depend on context.
Conversational implicature is meaning suggested but not stated, inferred through Grice’s maxims.
Analyse Hausa examples with recorded context and native-speaker checks, and avoid overgeneralising from one region or example.

en.title: Hausa Dialectology: Regional Variation and the Standard
en.short: Regional variation, isoglosses, dialect fieldwork, standard Hausa and attitudes to dialects.

sections.heading: Dialects and variation
sections.text: A dialect is a variety shared by a region or social group. Hausa varies in pronunciation, vocabulary and grammar across its wide speech area, especially in Nigeria and Niger. Speakers may differ in vowel length, tone, consonants, common words and plural or verb patterns. Mutual understanding usually remains high, but variation is real. Scholars group Hausa dialects differently; commonly named varieties include Kano, Katsina, Sokoto, Bauchi and Zaria. Boundaries are gradual, so no list is final.

sections.heading: Mapping isoglosses
sections.text: An isogloss is a line on a dialect map where one feature stops and another begins. Features include a pronunciation, a word or a grammatical form. A bundle of isoglosses often marks a dialect area, but lines rarely coincide exactly. A researcher may map the plural pattern used for a class of nouns. If towns east of a line prefer one pattern and towns west prefer another, that line is a morphological isogloss. The map shows a tendency, not a strict border.

sections.heading: Collecting and comparing
sections.text: Dialect data are collected by fieldwork: recording interviews, reading word lists and asking about everyday usage. Good practice uses matched speakers of similar background, the same prompts and careful transcription of tone and vowel length. Comparison lists features for each place and maps them. A small case: ten speakers from each of two towns read the same list. If eight in one town use a different plural form from eight in the other, the difference is worth testing with more speakers. Small samples suggest patterns; they do not prove them.

sections.heading: Standard and attitudes
sections.text: A standard variety is the form promoted in schools, dictionaries, broadcasting and official writing. Standard Hausa is based largely on Kano usage, but committees, writers, broadcasters and publishers shaped it. Standardisation is therefore social and political, not simply linguistic. It selects some features and sidelines others. Attitudes follow: standard forms may be seen as correct or educated, local forms as rustic. Linguists treat all dialects as systematic. Describe variation without ranking speakers.

keyPoints: A dialect is a regional or social variety; Hausa varies in sounds, words and grammar.
An isogloss marks the boundary of one feature, and bundles of isoglosses suggest dialect areas.
Dialect fieldwork uses matched speakers, common prompts and careful transcription of tone and vowel length.
Comparison lists and maps features; small samples suggest patterns but cannot prove them.
Standard Hausa is based largely on Kano usage and was shaped by education, writing and broadcasting.
Standardisation is a social process that selects features, so attitudes to dialects vary and no variety is linguistically inferior.

en.title: Historical and Comparative Linguistics of Hausa
en.short: Hausa in Chadic, the comparative method, sound correspondences, loanwords and contact evidence.

sections.heading: Hausa within Afroasiatic
sections.text:
Hausa belongs to the Afroasiatic family. Standard classifications divide it into six branches: Berber, Chadic, Cushitic, Egyptian, Omotic and Semitic. Chadic languages are spoken across northern Nigeria and around the Lake Chad basin, mainly in Nigeria, with others in Niger, Chad and Cameroon, and the branch contains well over a hundred languages.

Within Chadic, Hausa is usually placed in West Chadic, subgroup A. Its closest relative is generally taken to be Gwandara, a small language of central Nigeria. This follows Paul Newman’s classification. Hausa is unusual among Chadic languages for its long written tradition and its wide use as a trade language.

sections.heading: The comparative method
sections.text:
The comparative method compares words of probable common origin, called cognates, across related languages. Regular sound matches across many words form a sound correspondence, and these point to an earlier sound in the proto-language.

The steps are: propose cognates, list correspondences, reconstruct proto-sounds, then test the result. A common illustration is Hausa f where many Chadic languages have p, so reconstructions often derive Hausa f from an earlier *p. The asterisk marks a reconstructed, unattested form.

Caution is needed. Similar words may be borrowed or may resemble each other by chance. Many Chadic languages are poorly documented, and reconstructions by Newman and by Herrmann Jungraithmayr differ in detail. Treat any single reconstruction as a hypothesis.

sections.heading: Loanwords and contact
sections.text:
Loanwords are both evidence and a trap. Hausa has a large Arabic layer from trade and Islamic scholarship: malami (teacher) from Arabic muʿallim, with the ʿayn lost, and ilimi (knowledge) from ʿilm. English gives newer words such as mota (car), from motor. Kanuri, and French in Niger, have also contributed.

Loanwords show which languages Hausa has met, and roughly when. But a borrowed word can look like a cognate and distort a reconstruction, so each word’s history must be checked.

sections.heading: Evidence and limits
sections.text:
Other evidence comes from internal reconstruction, which uses irregularities inside Hausa; from comparing modern dialects; from Ajami manuscripts; and from place names. Each source has limits: old spellings are not phonetic, and dialects may themselves have borrowed.

Mark reconstructions with the asterisk, name the system you follow, and say plainly when a form is uncertain.

keyPoints: Hausa is a West Chadic language within Afroasiatic, and Gwandara is usually taken as its closest relative.
The comparative method uses regular sound correspondences among cognates to reconstruct proto-sounds.
An asterisk marks a reconstructed form that is not attested in any text.
Hausa f often corresponds to p in other Chadic languages, a common illustration of reconstruction.
Arabic, English, Kanuri and French loanwords show contact history but can mislead reconstruction.
Chadic reconstructions are hypotheses and differ between scholars, so state which system you follow.

en.title: Hausa Lexicography and Dictionary Making
en.short: Dictionary types, entry structure, tone marking, corpora, planning and evaluating Hausa dictionaries.

sections.heading: Types and users
sections.text: Lexicography is the planning, compiling and editing of dictionaries. Dictionary type follows users and purpose. A monolingual Hausa dictionary defines Hausa in Hausa; a bilingual dictionary pairs Hausa with English or another language; a multilingual dictionary covers several. Learner dictionaries use simple definitions and many examples. Historical dictionaries trace earlier forms and meanings. Descriptive dictionaries record usage; prescriptive ones recommend it. State the aim in the front matter.

sections.heading: Entry structure
sections.text: An entry has a headword, also called a lemma, in its citation form. It gives pronunciation and tone, part of speech, sense numbers, definitions, examples, labels such as dialect, and cross-references. Homographs, words spelt alike, need separate numbers. Definitions should be clear, not circular, and use simpler words than the headword. A good definition states the class and the distinguishing feature. Examples show natural use and help the reader choose the right sense.

sections.heading: Tone, examples, corpora
sections.text: Hausa tone and vowel length can change meaning, so a dictionary must mark them or state why it does not. Conventions vary: many use an acute accent for high tone and a grave accent for low tone, with length shown separately. The front matter explains every symbol. A corpus, a text collection, gives evidence for senses, frequency and natural examples. Concordances, word-in-context lines, help lexicographers compare uses. Examples may be corpus citations or edited sentences, but must be accurate and natural.

sections.heading: Planning and culture
sections.text: Planning starts with users, purpose, size, sources, team, budget and a style guide. A Kano team planning a school dictionary would choose subject terms, collect a balanced corpus, draft sample entries and test them with teachers. Evaluation checks coverage, accuracy, consistency, tone marking, clarity, examples and cross-references. Cultural terms are hard because they may lack an exact English equivalent. A local food, title or farm tool may need a descriptive definition, a loanword, a gloss or an illustration. Forced equivalence misleads; a cross-reference is safer.

keyPoints: Lexicography is the planning, compiling and editing of dictionaries for stated users and purposes.
Dictionary type follows users and purpose, whether monolingual, bilingual, learner or historical.
An entry normally gives headword, tone and pronunciation, part of speech, senses, definitions, examples and cross-references.
Hausa tone and vowel length must be marked consistently, and the front matter must explain the symbols.
A corpus supplies evidence for senses, frequency and natural examples.
Evaluation checks coverage, accuracy, consistency, clarity and usability, and cultural terms often need description or gloss rather than forced equivalence.

en.title: Translation and Interpreting: Hausa and English
en.short: Theory and practice of Hausa-English translation, equivalence, culture, register, interpreting and ethics.

sections.heading: Translation and meaning
sections.text: Translation is written transfer; interpreting is spoken or signed transfer. Equivalence means matching meaning and effect, not words. Formal equivalence keeps source form; dynamic equivalence aims at the same effect on the target audience. Word-for-word translation often fails because Hausa and English differ in grammar, idiom and tone. A literal version can be grammatical but misleading. In a Kano clinic, Amina translates a dehydration leaflet. She explains the treatment in familiar words instead of keeping an English medical phrase.

sections.heading: Culture and register
sections.text: Cultural terms, or realia, name things specific to a culture, such as food, titles or religious practices. They may have no exact English equivalent. Strategies include borrowing the term, calque (translating its parts), paraphrase, adaptation to the target setting, explicitation (adding needed information) and compensation (making up a loss elsewhere). Register is the level of formality and social relation. Audience matters: a legal document, radio drama and school book need different language. Hausa tone can change meaning, and tone marks are often omitted in ordinary writing, so check context and consult speakers.

sections.heading: Interpreting modes
sections.text: Interpreting modes differ by setting. Consecutive interpreting: the speaker pauses and the interpreter renders a segment, often using notes. Simultaneous interpreting: the interpreter speaks near real time, usually with equipment. Liaison or community interpreting: short turns in clinics, police stations or schools. Sight translation is reading a written text aloud in the other language. Preparation in terminology, names and procedure improves accuracy. Interpreting is demanding because there is no time to revise.

sections.heading: Ethics and limits
sections.text: Professional ethics require accuracy, confidentiality, impartiality, competence and boundaries. Interpreters should not add advice or omit uncomfortable facts. If a term is unclear, they ask for clarification. High-risk texts need checking, such as back-translation, where another person translates the target text back into the source language. No translation is perfect. The skopos, or purpose, guides choices: a news summary differs from a sworn court record. Translators state limits and refuse work beyond competence.

keyPoints: Equivalence means matching meaning and effect, not matching words one by one.
Word-for-word translation fails when grammar, idiom or tone differ between Hausa and English.
Cultural terms often need borrowing, paraphrase, explicitation or adaptation.
Register and audience decide whether language is formal, technical or plain.
Consecutive, simultaneous and liaison interpreting need different skills and preparation.
Professional ethics require accuracy, confidentiality, impartiality and competence.

en.title: Sociolinguistics of Hausa: Language, Society and Variation
en.short: How social factors shape Hausa use: multilingualism, code-switching, registers, variation and small studies.

sections.heading: Language and society
sections.text:
Sociolinguistics studies how society shapes language and how language marks social life. Hausa is spoken in several countries, especially Nigeria and Niger, and many speakers are multilingual. Multilingualism means using more than one language in daily life. A speaker may use Hausa at home, English at school and Arabic in religious settings. Each variety may be tied to a domain, a typical setting or activity.

Code-switching is moving between languages or varieties within a conversation. It can mark a topic change, show group membership or fill a gap. It follows social and grammatical patterns; it is not confusion.

sections.heading: Registers and social meaning
sections.text:
Register is a variety chosen for a situation or purpose, such as formal speech, classroom talk or market talk. Slang is informal vocabulary used by a group, often the young, to signal identity. Honorifics are forms that show respect or status, such as titles for elders or leaders.

Gender and generation differences are real but not absolute. Some young speakers use more English or new slang; older speakers may keep older forms. Women and men may differ in politeness, but class, education and setting often matter more. Avoid treating any group as uniform.

sections.heading: Urban and rural variation
sections.text: Urban and rural settings differ in contact, schooling, migration and media. City speakers may meet more languages and styles, so switching and slang can be common. Rural use may keep local forms. Variation also depends on trade, travel and education, so do not assume a simple town-versus-village split.

sections.heading: Designing a small study
sections.text:
Start with a clear question, such as how young speakers switch in family talk. Choose a setting and a small sample. Ask for consent, record naturally, and transcribe. Code each switch by type and by speaker. Compare groups, but report limits.

Example: Amina records 20 remarks from older relatives and 20 from classmates. If 8 of the 20 classmate remarks contain a switch, the rate is 8 ÷ 20 = 40%. She must not claim this represents all Hausa youth.

keyPoints: Sociolinguistics links language variation to social setting and identity.
Multilingualism and code-switching are normal, patterned parts of Hausa use.
Register, slang and honorifics carry social meaning and depend on relationship and setting.
Gender and generation differences are tendencies, not fixed rules; class and education also matter.
Urban and rural variation reflects contact, migration, schooling and media, not a simple split.
Small studies need a clear question, consent, careful recording, coding and honest limits.

en.title: Language Planning and Hausa in Education
en.short: Hausa’s status in Nigeria, Niger and beyond, mother-tongue policy and how it shapes teaching.

sections.heading: Three kinds of planning
sections.text:
Language planning is deliberate effort to change a language’s form or its role in society. Heinz Kloss separated status planning, which decides where a language is used, such as school, court or radio, from corpus planning, which develops the language itself through spelling, vocabulary and dictionaries. Acquisition planning concerns who learns it and when.

A policy on paper is only a start; teachers, books and examinations decide the outcome.

sections.heading: Nigeria: policy and practice
sections.text:
Nigeria’s official language is English. The National Policy on Education (1977, revised since) says the medium in pre-primary and the first three years of primary should be the child’s mother tongue or the language of the immediate community. For most pupils in Kano or Katsina that means Hausa. A 2022 national language policy extends mother-tongue medium to Primary 6, though implementation is uneven. Hausa is also a secondary school subject, and the 1999 Constitution allows the National Assembly to use Hausa, Igbo and Yoruba once arrangements are made.

In practice many classrooms turn to English earlier, because examinations and textbooks are in English.

sections.heading: Niger and beyond
sections.text: Niger’s official language is French, but Hausa is its most widely spoken first language. Since the 1970s Niger has run bilingual primary programmes that begin in a national language and add French gradually. Hausa is also a trade language in Benin, Togo, Ghana, Chad, Cameroon and Sudan, where it is usually a market or minority language and seldom a school subject. The same language carries a different status in each country.

sections.heading: What this does to teaching
sections.text:
Policy reaches the classroom through materials and assessment. Where Hausa is the medium, teachers need a settled orthography, reading schemes and subject textbooks. Where it is only a subject, they need grammar and literature books. Examinations decide much: if the final paper is in English, teaching drifts to English whatever the policy says.

A Primary 2 class in Kano and one in Maradi may both start in Hausa. The Kano child later switches to English, the Maradi child to French. The point of switch often matters more than the starting language.

keyPoints: Language planning is deliberate; Kloss divided it into status planning, which sets where a language is used, and corpus planning, which develops its spelling and vocabulary.

Nigeria’s National Policy on Education calls for the mother tongue or language of the immediate community as the medium in the first three years of primary school; a 2022 policy extends this to Primary 6.
English is Nigeria’s official language and French is Niger’s, so Hausa’s place in schooling differs between the two countries.
Niger has run bilingual primary programmes beginning in a national language, Hausa among them, since the 1970s.
Implementation depends on textbooks, teacher training and examinations; a final examination in English pulls teaching towards English.
Where Hausa is a trade or minority language, as in Ghana or Benin, it is seldom a school subject.

en.title: Hausa Prose Fiction
en.short: The Hausa novel and short story: history, themes, technique, audience and links to oral storytelling.

sections.heading: Emergence
sections.text: Hausa prose fiction is written narrative in Hausa, mainly the novel and short story. It grew in the twentieth century with print, schools, newspapers and literary competitions. Abubakar Imam’s Ruwan Bagaja appeared in 1934. Abubakar Tafawa Balewa wrote Shehu Umar in the 1930s, but it was published later, in 1955. They drew on oral tales, Islamic teaching and new reading publics. Short stories later found outlets in newspapers, magazines, radio and school readers. Dates vary, so check a literary history.

sections.heading: Themes and audience
sections.text: Recurring themes include marriage and family, education, migration, poverty, corruption, religion, gender and the tension between custom and modernity. Setting ranges from village and market town to Kano or Zaria and to historical Sokoto. Audience matters: school pupils, adult readers, radio listeners and later film audiences. Writers often address a moral question, not only tell a story.

sections.heading: Technique and character
sections.text: Narrative technique means how the story is told: who narrates, in what order, and with what distance and address. Early Hausa novels often use an omniscient narrator, one who knows all the characters’ thoughts, plus direct address, proverbs and journeys in episodes. Later fiction uses a first-person narrator, a character who says I, and more dialogue. Character can be flat, built around one trait, or round, shown changing. Close reading asks how names, speech, setting and repeated images guide judgement. In Shehu Umar, the capture and travel scenes let the reader trace the hero’s loss, endurance and return.

sections.heading: Orality and reading
sections.text: Written fiction is in dialogue with oral storytelling. It borrows folktale motifs, proverbs, songs, repeated openings and a performed narrator who may address the audience. It also changes them: print fixes a text, allows silent reading and invites new endings. Close reading should note the narrator’s voice, the use of Hausa proverbs, language mixing, setting details and the expected reader. Ask what the text expects the audience to know and what it teaches. Compare a written scene with an oral tale to see what is kept and what is reshaped.

keyPoints: Hausa prose fiction developed in the twentieth century through print, schooling, newspapers and competitions.
Early novels such as Ruwan Bagaja and Shehu Umar drew on oral and Islamic traditions.
Themes include marriage, education, migration, corruption, religion and custom versus modernity.
Narrative technique covers narrator, order, address, proverbs and episodic or plotted structure.
Character and setting guide moral judgement, and audience shapes style and publication.
Written fiction borrows from oral storytelling but also changes it through print and silent reading.

en.title: Hausa Poetry: Oral and Written
en.short: Metre, rhyme, imagery and performance in Hausa praise, religious and political poetry.

sections.heading: Sound and metre
sections.text: Hausa poetry is composed to be heard, even when written. Metre is the patterned arrangement of syllables and vowel length in a line. Rhythm is the felt beat produced by that pattern, by stress and by pauses. Rhyme is the matching of sounds, usually at line ends but also inside lines. Scansion is the careful marking of syllables, long and short vowels, pauses and rhyme. For example, mark two lines syllable by syllable, note long vowels, and check whether their final sounds match. Conventions differ by genre and region, so scan several lines before deciding a pattern. Do not assume English stress metre; Hausa poetry often depends on syllable count and vowel quantity.

sections.heading: Imagery and performance
sections.text: Imagery is the use of concrete pictures and comparisons to carry meaning. Praise poetry uses epithets, hyperbole and family or town names. Religious poetry uses Quranic allusion and moral exhortation. Political poetry can praise, warn or criticise leaders. Performance matters: a poem may be sung or chanted with instruments, a refrain and audience response. The performer’s voice, pauses and gestures shape meaning. A written text can therefore be one script for a performance, not the whole poem.

sections.heading: Praise, religion, politics
sections.text: Praise poetry is associated with praise singers and courtly or public occasions. Religious poetry, often linked to Islamic scholarship, teaches doctrine and devotion. Political poetry comments on authority and community. These categories overlap: a praise poem may be religious, and a religious poem may criticise rulers. The poet’s social role varies from entertainer and record-keeper to teacher, adviser and critic. Patronage, meaning support from rulers or sponsors, and audience expectations influence what can be said.

sections.heading: Oral and written
sections.text: Oral and written traditions feed each other. Oral poems are performed, remembered and transmitted; written poems use Arabic script (Ajami) or Roman script (Boko). Many written poems are still recited or sung, and oral poems are collected in books and recordings. Print, radio and later media widened circulation. When studying a poem, ask who performs it, for whom, in what setting, and whether the text is a transcript or a composition for reading.

keyPoints: Hausa poetry is often performed, so metre, rhythm and voice matter.
Metre patterns syllables and vowel length; scansion marks these features.
Rhyme and imagery carry meaning and aid memory.
Praise, religious and political poetry overlap in social function.
Oral and written traditions interact through Ajami, Boko, print and recordings.
Poets may entertain, teach, advise or criticise, depending on patronage and audience.

en.title: Hausa Drama and Performance
en.short: Stage, radio, television and film drama in Hausa: structure, character, dialogue, audience and production.

sections.heading: Drama across media
sections.text: Hausa drama reaches audiences through stage, radio, television and film. Stage drama is performed live before an audience; radio drama is heard, so sound effects and speech carry the action; television and film drama are recorded and edited. Hausa film industry is often called Kannywood. Each medium changes what the audience can see, hear and do. A live play invites immediate reaction; a broadcast reaches people at home and can be replayed.

sections.heading: Structure and character
sections.text: Dramatic structure is the arrangement of action. A common pattern is exposition, rising action, climax and resolution. Exposition gives background; rising action builds conflict; the climax is the turning point; resolution shows the outcome. Character is built through what a figure says, does and wants, and what others say. A protagonist carries the main desire, while an antagonist blocks it. In a short radio play, a character must be established quickly through voice and reported action.

sections.heading: Dialogue and audience
sections.text: Dialogue is speech between characters. Good dialogue does more than give information: it reveals feeling, status and conflict. Hausa drama may use registers from formal speech to market talk, and tone matters. The audience is not passive. A stage crowd may laugh, murmur or stay silent, and actors adjust. Broadcast audiences are unseen, so producers imagine them and use signals such as music or a pause to guide response.

sections.heading: Text and event
sections.text: Analyse a play or programme in two ways. As text, ask about plot, character, dialogue, theme and language. As event, ask who performed, where, for whom, with what technology and constraints. Production covers script, rehearsal, direction, design, sound, camera and editing. Context shapes meaning: the same line can seem comic on stage and serious on radio. Imagine a radio play set in Kano: a trader, Malam Sani, hides a debt from his wife, Hauwa. His worry must come through dialogue and sound. On stage, posture and audience silence would add meaning.

keyPoints: Hausa drama is made for stage, radio, television and film, and each medium changes what the audience can see and hear.
Dramatic structure usually moves through exposition, rising action, climax and resolution.
Character is revealed by speech, action, desire and the comments of others.
Dialogue carries information, feeling, status and conflict, and tone matters.
Performance context, including place, audience, technology and production, shapes meaning.
Analyse a drama both as text and as event, that is, as a script and as a performance.

en.title: Literary Criticism and Theory for Hausa Literature
en.short: Main critical approaches applied to Hausa oral and written texts, with argument-building and fair comparison.

sections.heading: Approaches
sections.text:
Criticism is reasoned interpretation, not summary. Formalism, or close reading, studies how a text works through image, repetition, structure and word choice. Narratology asks who narrates, what is told, and in what order. Stylistics uses linguistic description to explain effects of tone, rhythm and diction.

Reader-response criticism studies how actual readers and audiences make meaning. Marxist criticism asks whose interests a text serves. Postcolonial criticism examines colonial power and resistance. Feminist criticism asks how gender shapes representation and reception. Performance criticism adds audience, occasion and voice.

sections.heading: Text and context
sections.text:
Use these approaches on both oral and written Hausa texts. Narrative has two layers: story, what happens, and discourse, how it is told. Ask who speaks, who sees, and what is left out. Genre is a recognised kind, such as proverb, praise poem, folktale, novel or play; it sets expectations.

Style is the writer’s or performer’s characteristic use of language. Audience includes the implied reader built into the text and the real listeners at a performance. Ideology means the values and power relations a text assumes or challenges.

sections.heading: Building an argument
sections.text:
Build an argument in four steps. State a clear claim about the text. Give evidence: a line, scene, image, formula or performance detail. Explain how the evidence supports the claim using a named approach. Answer a likely objection.

For example, suppose a student claims a praise poem unites the community. She cites repeated praise names and the audience’s response, then notes that the poem also flatters a patron. A fair reading can hold both points.

sections.heading: Comparing views
sections.text:
Compare perspectives by stating each view’s assumption, evidence and limit. A formalist may show how repetition creates unity; a Marxist may ask who benefits from that unity. Do not call one view wrong before testing it.

Ask what each explains well and what it ignores. In Hausa studies, oral performance and written texts often need more than one approach. Your conclusion should weigh the readings, not simply list them.

keyPoints: Criticism is reasoned interpretation supported by evidence from the text or performance.
Formalism, narratology, stylistics, reader-response, Marxist, postcolonial and feminist criticism ask different questions.
Narrative separates story from discourse; genre, style, audience and ideology shape meaning.
An argument needs a claim, evidence, explanation and a response to objection.
Compare perspectives by their assumptions, evidence and limits, not by labels.
Use more than one approach for Hausa oral and written texts when the text demands it.

en.title: Research Methods in Hausa Studies
en.short: Designing small Hausa research projects: questions, sources, fieldwork, ethics and reports.

sections.heading: Designing the project
sections.text: Start with a research question: a clear, answerable question that your small project can address. A good question names a population, place and issue, and it is not too broad. Write a short literature review to show what is already known and where your study fits. Then choose a design: interviews, observation, text analysis, archive work or a mix. State your aim, objectives and method in one page before collecting data.

sections.heading: Sources and fieldwork
sections.text: Primary sources are materials you collect or examine yourself, such as interviews, recordings, manuscripts or performances. Secondary sources are books and articles by other scholars. For interviews, prepare an interview guide, a list of open questions. Choose participants purposively, meaning by relevant criteria, and explain how you will find them. In fieldwork, record dates, places and speakers, and ask permission before recording. In archives, note call numbers and access rules. For example, a student in Kano studying praise poetry might interview three performers, record two performances and compare them with published texts.

sections.heading: Transcription and ethics
sections.text: Transcription turns speech into text. Decide whether to use Boko (Latin script) or Ajami (Arabic-based script), keep the original audio, and note pauses, overlaps and tone where relevant. Use a consistent file name and a data log. Ethics means informed consent: tell participants the purpose, how data will be used and stored, and their right to withdraw. Protect anonymity where promised. Seek permission for oral literature and archive material, and follow your department’s rules.

sections.heading: Writing and citing
sections.text: A proposal states the title, problem, question, objectives, literature, method, ethics, timeline and references. A report adds findings, analysis and discussion. Use one citation style consistently, such as APA or your department’s guide, and cite every source, including interviews with date and place. Keep consent forms and transcripts in an appendix or secure file. Check facts and quotations before submission.

keyPoints: A research question should be clear, answerable and narrow enough for a small project.
Primary sources are collected by you; secondary sources are other scholars’ books and articles.
Prepare an interview guide, choose participants by stated criteria and record dates, places and speakers.
Transcription requires consistent choices about script, tone and file naming, and the original audio should be kept.
Informed consent means explaining purpose, storage, use and the right to withdraw, and protecting anonymity where promised.
A proposal states problem, question, method, ethics and timeline; a report adds findings and uses one citation style consistently.

en.title: Hausa in the Media and Popular Culture
en.short: Hausa radio, TV, Kannywood film, music and social media: genre, style, audience and analysis.

sections.heading: Media landscape
sections.text:
Hausa media are not one system. They include radio and television in Nigeria and Niger, the Kannywood film industry of northern Nigeria, music recordings, and social media such as WhatsApp, Facebook, YouTube and TikTok. Each platform has its own reach and cost.

Radio serves rural and low-literacy audiences because it needs no reading. Television and film add image and sound. Social media allow quick comment but need data and devices.

sections.heading: Genres and style
sections.text:
A genre is a kind of text, such as news, call-in show, drama, song or film. Genres shape Hausa usage. Radio news tends toward formal speech; call-in shows allow interruption, laughter and accent. Drama and film use dialogue and proverbs. Music uses repetition and images. Social media mix writing with voice, images and video. Code-switching, moving between Hausa and English or Arabic (French in Niger), is common in advertising and youth talk.

Tone matters in audio; spelling matters in posts.

sections.heading: Advertising and debate
sections.text:
Advertising sells goods and ideas. It uses slogans, praise, humour and voices. A radio advert repeats a product name; a film shows a star using it. Public debate appears in call-in programmes, interviews and comment threads. Presenters manage turn-taking, and participants may appeal to religion or custom.

In an invented Kano call-in show on school fees, a parent speaks in Hausa, a teacher answers in formal Hausa with English terms, and the presenter summarises. This shows register shifting by role.

sections.heading: Analysing texts
sections.text:
To analyse a media text, ask who made it, for which audience, on which platform and in which region. Identify the genre and rules. Note language choices: formal or informal register, code-switching, dialect features, proverbs, tone and images. Ask what the text assumes, who speaks, who is silent, and how advertising or sponsorship shapes it.

Compare one story on radio, film and WhatsApp. Do not treat one platform as typical of Hausa media. Check figures against sources.

keyPoints: Hausa media include radio, television, Kannywood film, music and social media, each with different reach and rules.
Genres such as news, call-in shows, drama and advertising shape register, code-switching and tone.
Radio remains important for rural and low-literacy audiences because it needs no reading.
Advertising and public debate show audience, sponsorship and social values.
Analyse media texts by producer, genre, audience, platform, region and language choices.
Do not generalise from one platform; compare radio, film and social media.

en.title: Islamic Scholarship and Hausa Literature
en.short: Islamic learning, Ajami texts, Arabic genres and the religious-secular mix in Hausa literature.

sections.heading: Literacy and Islamic learning
sections.text:
