Islamic scholarship gave many Hausa communities a written culture before Latin-script schooling became widespread. Teachers in Quranic schools taught reading and memorisation of Arabic texts. From this setting Hausa writers adapted the Arabic script to write Hausa. This adapted script is called Ajami. It was used for religious works, letters, records and poetry. Boko, the Latin-based script, later became the main script of formal education and publishing, especially in northern Nigeria. Ajami remained important in religious and personal writing.

This history matters because Hausa literacy was not only a product of colonial or Western education. Islamic learning created readers, writers and patrons.

sections.heading: Ajami genres
sections.text:
Ajami literature includes verse and prose. Much of it is devotional: praise of the Prophet, moral instruction, elegies and didactic poems used in teaching. Prose works include sermons, commentaries and translations of religious knowledge. Arabic genres and Arabic loanwords shaped this writing. For example, Hausa religious vocabulary contains many Arabic borrowings, and genres such as tafsir, Quran commentary, have parallels in Hausa scholarship.

But Ajami was also practical. People wrote contracts, letters, remedies and local histories in it. A student should therefore treat Ajami as a medium, not as a single religious genre.

sections.heading: Religious and secular writing
sections.text:
Hausa literature cannot be reduced to religion. Oral poetry, folktales, proverbs and praise songs have their own histories, and modern prose fiction, drama and media writing draw on many sources. Islamic learning shaped themes, images and conventions, but secular writers also use them critically or playfully. Secular here means writing not mainly concerned with religious teaching.

A case: suppose a student finds a handwritten Ajami poem in a family collection. It may begin as moral advice, yet mention a market dispute or a local ruler. Reading it historically means asking who wrote it, for whom, and in what setting, not assuming every line is doctrine. Printed Hausa novels quoting religious verse need the same care.

keyPoints: Islamic learning created a written Hausa culture through Ajami, the Arabic-based script.
Ajami texts include devotional poetry, didactic prose, sermons, letters and local records.
Arabic genres and loanwords shaped Hausa religious registers and literary forms.
Hausa literature also has oral, secular and modern genres not defined by religion.
Read Ajami and religious texts historically: ask about author, audience, setting and purpose.
Do not treat all Hausa writing as religious; religion is one influence among many.

en.title: Advanced Hausa Phonology and Morphosyntax
en.short: Competing analyses of Hausa tone, prosody, word structure and clause structure, with study design.

sections.heading: Tone and prosody
sections.text: Hausa uses high and low tones to distinguish words and grammatical forms. A central debate is whether a falling pitch on a long vowel is one contour tone, a pitch that moves within a syllable, or a sequence of high plus low. Evidence comes from minimal pairs, downstep (a step down in pitch after a high tone), and acoustic measurements of fundamental frequency (F0, the physical pitch). Autosegmental phonology treats tones as separate units linked to tone-bearing units; rival accounts treat some pitch patterns as prosodic. Prosody is the organisation of pitch, length and rhythm above the sound. Each analysis predicts different phrase-edge and focus patterns.

sections.heading: Words and morphosyntax
sections.text: Word structure debates ask whether aspect markers and pronouns are separate words, clitics or affixes. A clitic is a small word-like element that depends phonologically on a neighbour. Hausa verb forms also raise the question of how much of the grade system, the numbered classes of verb forms, is morphological and how much phonological. Morphosyntax is the study of how word forms and sentence structure interact. Evidence includes order, agreement, tone changes and separability.

sections.heading: Clause structure
sections.text: Clause structure analyses disagree about the basic skeleton of the Hausa sentence and the place of focus and relative constructions. Constituent structure is the grouping of words into phrases. One view posits a rich functional layer above the verb phrase; another uses construction-based templates. Evidence includes word order, resumptive pronouns (pronouns that fill the gap left by a moved phrase), agreement and tone. A good argument states its predictions and tests them against minimal contrasts, not just a few examples.

sections.heading: Reading and study design
sections.text: To design a small theoretical study, choose one puzzle, state two competing analyses, and derive a testable prediction. For example, test whether a falling pitch is a contour tone by comparing long and short vowels in controlled frames, recording several speakers, measuring F0, and checking dialect and speaker variation. Read critically by separating data from interpretation, looking for confounds, and asking whether another analysis explains the same facts more simply.

keyPoints: Hausa tone analyses must separate lexical tone from prosodic and grammatical pitch effects.
The contour-tone debate turns on whether falling pitch is one unit or a high-low sequence.
Downstep and F0 evidence can support or weaken competing tone analyses.
Word-structure debates ask whether aspect markers and pronouns are words, clitics or affixes.
Clause-structure claims should be tested against focus, relative and resumptive-pronoun data.
A small theoretical study states rival analyses, derives predictions and controls dialect and speaker variation.

en.title: Advanced Literary Theory and Comparative Poetics
en.short: Theories of oral and written literature, performance, genre and translation, applied to Hausa texts in comparison.

sections.heading: Theory and comparison
sections.text:
Comparative poetics studies ideas about what literature is, how it is made and how it affects audiences across African and world traditions. It does not assume that English terms such as fiction, drama or poetry fit every tradition.

Use etic terms, the analyst’s categories, with care, and record emic terms, the community’s own names. A theoretical argument states a question, defines its terms, chooses texts for a stated reason, and explains why they can be compared.

sections.heading: Orality and performance
sections.text:
Oral literature is composed, remembered and received in performance. Formulaic theory, associated with Milman Parry and Albert Lord, shows how repeated phrases and themes help oral poets compose in real time. Performance theory asks about audience, setting, voice and gesture, not only words on a page.

A Hausa oral poem may change in each telling; a written Hausa novel may still be read aloud. Written texts invite reception theory, which studies how readers make meaning. Compare like with like: a recorded performance is not the same as a printed text.

sections.heading: Genre and translation
sections.text:
Genre is a convention that guides writers and readers, not a fixed box. Translation adds another layer. Metre, tone, formula, praise name and religious allusion may resist transfer. Comparative claims must say which text and which translation were used.

Case: if a student compares a Hausa praise poem with a southern African praise poem, shared praise must be shown through function and occasion, not assumed from the English label.

sections.heading: Framing the argument
sections.text:
Frame an argument in five moves: pose a clear question; define the categories; describe the corpus and its language; justify comparability; state the limits of the evidence.

Test imported theory against the text and revise it. Do not rank traditions. Name your own position and the translation’s limits. The aim is a defensible comparison, not a universal law.

keyPoints: Comparative poetics compares ideas about literature without assuming one tradition’s categories are universal.
Distinguish etic analytical terms from emic terms used by the community.
Oral literature is best studied as performance, including audience, setting and voice.
Genre is a convention, and translation changes metre, tone and allusion.
Justify comparability by function and occasion, not by an English label.
Frame an argument by defining terms, describing the corpus and stating limits.

en.title: Language Contact and Change in Hausa
en.short: Arabic, English, French and African contact; borrowing versus code-switching; attitudes and shift.

sections.heading: Contact history
sections.text: Hausa has long contact with Arabic through Islamic scholarship, trade and Ajami writing, and with English through British colonial rule in Nigeria and later education and media. In Niger, French has long been the official language and still influences Hausa in administration and schooling. Contact with Kanuri, Fulfulde, Tuareg and other neighbours also left traces. Contact is not one-way: Hausa is a lingua franca and has influenced neighbouring languages. Religious vocabulary often shows Arabic influence; technology and administration often show English or French influence.

sections.heading: Borrowing or switching
sections.text: A loanword is borrowed from another language and integrated into Hausa phonology, morphology and ordinary usage. Code-switching is the alternation of two languages within a conversation or clause by a bilingual speaker. Borrowing is community-level and often permanent; code-switching is discourse-level and may be transient. The boundary is a matter of degree. A form may begin as a switch and become a loan. Test integration: monolingual use, phonological adaptation, frequency and whether it fills a lexical gap.

sections.heading: Evaluating contact data
sections.text: Contact claims need evidence. Ask who recorded the data, when, where and in what genre. Check whether tone and vowel length were marked, because Hausa meaning depends on them. Compare dictionaries and corpora. Suppose a Kano radio interview contains English “computer” inside a Hausa clause. If the speaker is bilingual, uses it once and returns to English, treat it as code-switching. If older monolingual speakers use an adapted form in everyday Hausa, it is likely a loan.

sections.heading: Attitudes and shift
sections.text: Language attitudes shape contact outcomes. Arabic may carry religious prestige, English or French educational and economic prestige, and Hausa local identity. Positive attitudes can encourage borrowing; negative attitudes can resist it. Language shift means a community gradually uses another language in more domains, often across generations. Hausa is expanding as a lingua franca in some areas while some Hausa speakers shift to English or French in elite, official or diaspora settings. Do not infer shift from a few switches; examine domain use, intergenerational transmission and reports.

keyPoints: Hausa contact with Arabic, English, French and neighbouring languages differs by domain and region.
A loanword is integrated into Hausa and used by monolinguals; code-switching is bilingual alternation in discourse.
The boundary between borrowing and switching is gradual, so test frequency, adaptation and monolingual use.
Evaluate contact data by source, date, place, genre and tone marking.
Attitudes can encourage or resist borrowing, but shift must be shown by domain use and intergenerational transmission.
Hausa can expand as a lingua franca while some speakers shift to English or French in certain settings.

en.title: Research Methods and Dissertation Design in Hausa Studies
en.short: Proposal, literature review, framework, sampling, fieldwork, ethics, transcription, writing for a master’s dissertation.

sections.heading: From topic to proposal
sections.text:
A master’s dissertation is built around one clear main question that others can check. Narrow a broad interest into a research problem: not "Hausa proverbs" but, for example, how young speakers in one town use proverbs in WhatsApp messages. Break the main question into two or three sub-questions, state the gap, and set a scope you can finish in the time allowed.

A proposal usually covers background, problem, questions, literature, framework, methods, ethics and a timeline; length varies by department. Committees judge feasibility above ambition.

sections.heading: Reading and framework
sections.text:
A literature review is an argument, not a list. Group earlier work by theme, say what each study found, and show the gap yours fills. Cite primary sources and check page numbers.

A theoretical framework is the set of ideas that shapes your questions and explains findings. A study of oral performance might use the oral-formulaic theory of Milman Parry and Albert Lord; a study of variation might use quantitative sociolinguistics. Name the framework, define its terms, and say how you apply it.

sections.heading: Fieldwork, archives, ethics
sections.text:
Sampling is choosing whom to study and defending the choice. Probability sampling gives every member of a defined population a known chance of selection; purposive sampling selects people for a stated reason and does not support statistical generalisation. Interviewing 80 of 400 registered members is 80 ÷ 400 = 20 per cent, one in five.

Archival work means reading documents where they are held: manuscripts in Ajami script, colonial reports, newspapers, court records. Record catalogue numbers and permissions.

Ethics means informed consent, the right to withdraw, confidentiality, and agreed rights with performers before recording.

sections.heading: Transcription and writing
sections.text:
Transcribe consistently: fix a convention for orthography, tone and vowel length marking, and pauses, and keep the raw recording. Analysis means coding material into themes and testing them against the whole corpus.

Write early, chapter by chapter, and keep a log of decisions. Set weekly targets and leave time for revision.

keyPoints: A dissertation needs one clear, checkable main research question and a scope you can finish.
A literature review argues for a gap; it does not summarise sources one by one.
The theoretical framework shapes the questions and explains the findings.
Probability sampling allows generalisation; purposive sampling does not.
Ethics requires consent, the right to withdraw, confidentiality, and agreed rights over recordings.
Transcription conventions must be fixed and applied consistently to every recording.
